title: The 8 Levels of First Job Salary
house: A bustling neon-lit corporate metropolis named Citrus City, where rain slicked pavement reflects towering glass skyscrapers and fruit and vegetable people rush between subway stations and high-rise cubicles.
catchphrase: The number on your forehead never lies.
links: A quiet man in a sharp suit leaves a massive tip at the subway kiosk in Level 1 and Level 5.
The stressed barista from Level 2 is spotted crying in the corporate elevator in Level 6.
A dropped golden coin rolls past the reception desk in every single level.

levels.open_loop: Why did the recruiter suddenly shred my contract right before my first shift?

gegenspieler.tat: Laughs at my unpaid internship offer and tells me to buy coffee for the real employees.

levels.name: Pip, 22, Intern
levels.story: The 8 levels of first job salary. Level 1. Level 1: 0 dollars a month and they expect me to work eighty hours a week for exposure. I stood in the glass-walled HR lobby holding my cold resume, my forehead glowing with a stark zero. You are working for free because you are worth nothing to this company. My chest tightened into a knot of burning humiliation and I swallowed hard. We don't take charity cases here, kid. You'll see that in Level 2.

levels.name: Zoe, 24, Junior Analyst
levels.story: The 8 levels of first job salary. Level 2. Level 2: 2,400 dollars a month and rent takes two thirds before I even buy groceries. I sat in the cramped breakroom staring at my meager paycheck while sipping lukewarm tap water. You think staying late makes you special when your number is this pathetic? My eyes stung with hot tears of pure exhaustion and rage after three all-nighters. Know your place at the bottom of the ladder. You'll see that in Level 3.

levels.name: Leo, 26, Assistant
levels.story: The 8 levels of first job salary. Level 3. Level 3: 3,800 dollars a month and burnout is just another word for keeping your job. I stood at the industrial copy machine in the basement level, my eyes burning from spreadsheets. You want a raise with that mediocre output? My blood pressure spiked instantly as I dropped a stack of important tax forms on the floor. You are easily replaceable, kid. You'll see that in Level 4.

levels.name: Maya, 28, Project Manager
levels.story: The 8 levels of first job salary. Level 4. Level 4: 5,200 dollars a month and I finally thought I made it out of the struggle. I stood on the balcony of my new high-rise loft holding a glass of prosecco. Must be nice living high up while the rest of us drown in paperwork. A bitter knot formed in my stomach as I remembered how hard I fought for this title. Enjoy your view while it lasts. You'll see that in Level 5.

levels.name: Marcus, 35, Team Lead
levels.story: The 8 levels of first job salary. Level 5. Level 5: 7,100 dollars a month and every extra dollar just buys you more sleepless nights. I sat at the head of the mahogany conference table rubbing my temples as projections flashed. You must never worry about bills with a number like that, sir. A hollow laugh escaped my lips because my marriage was falling apart from overwork. Your team's numbers are slipping. You'll see that in Level 6.

levels.name: Barnaby, 42, Director
levels.story: The 8 levels of first job salary. Level 6. Level 6: 11,500 dollars a month and you realize power is just a cage made of gold. I paced across the plush Persian rug of my corner office, my phone buzzing with updates. Must be nice sitting up here while we do the real lifting. A cold wave of guilt washed over me because I barely remembered my children's faces. The board is initiating a hostile takeover. You'll see that in Level 7.

levels.story: The 8 levels of first job salary. Level 7. Level 7: 22,005 dollars a month and when you reach the top everybody wants to watch you fall. levels.name: Director Plum, 55, Founder
levels.story: The 8 levels of first job salary. Level 8. Level 8: 999,999 dollars a month and at the very top you realize the number was never yours to keep. I sat in the vaulted penthouse archive room surrounded by decades of employee records. You own the entire city, yet you look more miserable than the interns downstairs. A quiet chuckle escaped my lips because I had watched every fruit chase a glowing digit. The number on your forehead was never your worth; it was just a price tag they gave you.
